title: LawNext on Location: Visiting Everlaw's Headquarters For A Conversation with AJ Shankar, Founder and CEO
author: AJ Shankar

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: The source provides no substantive claims, evidence, reasoning or predictions with which to assess its stance toward cautious experimentation, customer–provider collaboration, distributed expertise or outcome-based trust.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Shankar reinforces the specialist-workflow thesis by identifying litigation-specific collaboration requirements and showing how legal domain expertise was accumulated through sustained practitioner input. He extends the cluster with a concrete architectural rationale—cloud elasticity for fluctuating discovery workloads—but does not substantively address generative AI, human verification or the durability of specialist layers against improving general models.
qs: Thousands of conversations now and you know in the company we have you know many many dozens of JD's and so on just accumulated over the years So having to build that out I would say there's a cost right of coming in coming that angle But I think I also knew that I was eager to learn about it.
And so the platform has to support all those kind of collaboration paradigms as an example of some of the complexity that doesn't exist in other industries.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Shankar accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI is jagged, augmentative and dependent on human verification. He materially develops it with a concrete deployment model: narrow, lower-hallucination use cases embedded in robust enterprise workflows, with grounded outputs, privacy controls and risk-based user rules.
qs: Develop use cases where we think there's a low likelihood of hallucination versus high and stay away from the high likelihood hallucination cases.
And then ensure that every outcome is tied back to something you can look at and check.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source broadly supports the cluster’s distinction between raw model capability and practical usefulness, while narrowing the need for specialist workflows by arguing that general-purpose models can already handle some simple transactional tasks. This is a scoped caveat, not a rejection of the cluster’s broader proposition about dependable legal work.
qs: stuff for the reason that you can record something that looks perfect but to actually make it useful is another thing entirely.
I do think for those kinds of simple transactional tasks, you can use a Claude coworker, what have you, and it'll do a pretty good job.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Shankar supports the cluster’s central lawyer-guided framing by rejecting any single-tool solution and presenting technology as something that must be combined with human intelligence. The excerpt is a general endorsement rather than a concrete extension: it offers no workflow examples, implementation detail or empirical evidence.
qs: I think there's no single tool to solve these problems.
You're going to have to solve, you are going to have to use a lot of technology and human intelligence to solve your problems.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: Shankar aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on practical utility over polished demonstrations and treats adoption as task-specific rather than evidence of wholesale lawyer replacement. His expectation of broader use for simple transactional tasks is supportive but predictive, with no workflow-level evaluation or verification evidence supplied.
qs: stuff for the reason that you can record something that looks perfect but to actually make it useful is another thing entirely.
I do think for those kinds of simple transactional tasks, you can use a Claude coworker, what have you, and it'll do a pretty good job.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: Shankar aligns with the cluster’s view that generative AI is strategically important but product development must remain grounded in workflow fit and practical user needs. His account supports customer-oriented differentiation, though it provides no evidence on development speed, build-versus-buy decisions, migration or integration constraints.
qs: And yeah, think generative AI is truly transformative in this way.
All I can do is look at our users' needs and what tools they need to solve their problems and focus on that, but it's gonna be an interesting time.

kp.k: Discovery requires complementary technologies, not a single AI solution
kp.d: Shankar characterises discovery as a difficult information-retrieval problem requiring multiple approaches. Everlaw's statistical machine learning, predictive coding and clustering remain useful alongside generative AI. He expects technology and human intelligence to remain complementary in the near term, rather than AI completing litigation work on its own.
qs: fundamentally discovery is at its heart a process of information retrieval, right? Finding the knowledge, the information that really matters.
You're going to have to solve, you are going to have to use a lot of technology and human intelligence to solve your problems. I don't think that's changing in the near term.

kp.k: Litigation platforms must support complex interorganisational collaboration
kp.d: Shankar identifies coordinated work, permissions, deadlines, administration and procurement as substantial challenges beyond document analysis. Platforms must accommodate multiple co-litigating firms, public-private litigation partnerships, and law firms working with their corporate clients. He presents this accumulated workflow infrastructure as an important part of litigation software's value.
qs: meaningful discovery efforts are highly coordinated collaborative efforts. And the way people work together is really complex.
You have different law firms litigating together, so you have to have the software to support that.
And of course, you have a law firm working with their in-house counsel that's paying their bills, right?

kp.k: Cloud scalability and usability remain central despite generative AI
kp.d: Shankar says cloud architecture addresses discovery's rapidly fluctuating data volumes, while approachable interfaces determine whether sophisticated capabilities are actually usable. He regards generative AI as a step change in analysis rather than a replacement for Everlaw's longstanding priorities of cloud infrastructure, ease of use and collaboration.
qs: Individual cases can spike in size or shrink in size overnight. Provisioning is really hard when you're working with machines you procured.
If you have every feature in the world, but your interface looks like an airplane cockpit with like 700 dials, people won't know how to use those features.
It is a step change in the kinds of analysis you can do with machine intelligence.

kp.k: AI design prioritises bounded tasks and verifiable outputs
kp.d: Shankar describes a vendor design philosophy that acknowledges generative AI's lower reliability relative to deterministic tools. Everlaw selects narrowly defined use cases, avoids uses it considers more prone to fabrication, integrates functionality into existing workflows and provides source citations for human checking. He asserts that grounding also improves performance, without presenting measured accuracy results.
qs: It's much more like a person, much more capable and expressive and fluid, but also less reliable.
Develop use cases where we think there's a low likelihood of hallucination versus high and stay away from the high likelihood hallucination cases.
And then ensure that every outcome is tied back to something you can look at and check.
Turns out that grounding its responses in this data also improves its performance, right?

kp.k: Privacy controls and client judgement underpin responsible adoption
kp.d: Shankar says Everlaw sought to prevent customer data from being retained by model providers or used for training, with controls allowing users to opt in or out. His 'smart intern' analogy emphasises user education about capabilities, limitations and verification. Clients and firms must determine appropriate uses according to their own risk tolerance; the vendor cannot make all these decisions for them.
qs: security and privacy and showing your data is never used in training.
It's never retained by these providers
you can opt in or opt out and have control over them.
it's not great, where you should check its work, where you should use it all the time, where you shouldn't use it at all, right?
it's something clients have to do as they develop their own risk tolerance and their firms determine kind of their AI journey.

kp.k: Generative AI extends across review and litigation preparation
kp.d: Shankar describes existing capabilities for summarisation, topic extraction, sentiment analysis, document questions, information extraction and coding suggestions across thousands or tens of thousands of documents. Coding suggestions apply a review rubric, explain reasoning and cite document passages for checking, including responsiveness and privilege issues. Other functions analyse depositions, identify conflicting testimony, draft memos and construct statements or tables of facts. His favourable assessment of performance is a vendor assertion, not a reported independent evaluation.
qs: you can summarize documents, extract topics, do sentiment analysis, you can ask a question of a document
you can do coding suggestions, as it's called, across... thousands or tens of thousands of documents
actually suggest which codes to apply, which ones not to apply, explain its reasoning, cite the relevant parts of the documents so you can check its work.
You can also use the AI to analyze depositions, ask questions of depositions, look for conflicting testimony, write memos, construct tables of facts.

kp.k: Deep Dive targets specific questions across large document collections
kp.d: Shankar says Deep Dive, released in December, retrieves documents, extracts and ranks facts, and synthesises source-grounded answers across a corpus. He reports use on hundreds of cases and describes answering specific questions within million-document collections in approximately one minute. Suggested applications include deposition preparation and testing whether newly uploaded documents support a fact. These are vendor-reported capabilities and adoption claims, not benchmark findings.
qs: the thing we released in December, the deep dive tool allows you to just ask a question of your whole corpus and have the AI cite, actually pull a number of documents, extract facts from them, rank those facts, and then actually synthesize an answer
now have it on hundreds of cases now.

But when you have a specific question and somewhere in your million documents is an answer, it is kind of a revelatory experience to go type your question in and in like one minute get an answer that's citing a specific document or set of documents.

kp.k: Targeted retrieval does not replace comprehensive responsiveness review
kp.d: Shankar explicitly limits Deep Dive to targeted information finding rather than broad responsiveness review, for which people or coding suggestions remain necessary. He says customers have found previously missed critical documents, but provides no direct customer testimony or systematic results in this transcript. He contrasts its question-based accessibility with predictive coding's expertise and training requirements.
qs: It's not meant for that. You need to do real review and you can use coding suggestions or people, what have you.
then I've turned on deep dive and have found critical documents they've missed.
Predictive coding, extremely powerful, but requires some expertise to set up and train and all that stuff.
To find something interesting, you have to have already found something interesting. Deep dive doesn't have any of those barriers.

kp.k: Document-grounded analysis differs from recalling legal authorities
kp.d: Shankar argues that models perform better when extracting and citing supplied context than when answering precise, high-stakes legal questions from training knowledge. He identifies invented case law as a risk and says Everlaw avoids relying on models' internal legal knowledge, instead grounding requests in supplied documents. He acknowledges that context-based performance is still imperfect and gives no measured hallucination rate.
qs: these tools do a good job at, if you feed it context, evaluating what's in that context, extracting information, citing back to it, not perfect, but a good job.
we stay away from this asking it about its own training knowledge of the law.
Everything we ask the AIs in Everlaw is really based on the four corners of the documents we have in hand that we feed to it at the time of asking the question.

kp.k: AI could widen or narrow access-to-justice disparities
kp.d: Shankar frames the distributional effects of litigation AI as conditional: exclusive access for well-resourced users could widen the justice gap, while access for users without means could enable otherwise unaffordable work. He reports millions of dollars of donated product in the preceding year through Everlaw's charitable programme, presenting this as part of its response rather than evidence of measured justice outcomes.
qs: if only users with means can use these tools, it can also decrease it because it allows users without the means to... do a lot of work that they couldn't otherwise afford.
Millions of dollars of product donated and we're going to see more of that as well.
you want to really have a level playing field where everyone has access to the truth.

kp.k: Buyers should test AI on real work
kp.d: Shankar considers generative AI transformative but acknowledges that buyers face competing vendor promises and unreliable demonstrations. He recommends direct trials, comparisons and use of real customer data, rather than trusting polished demonstrations. He explicitly disclaims perfect answers from Deep Dive and advocates human decision-making and control for repeatable, defensible work.
qs: Is it gonna answer every question perfectly? No, absolutely not.
Put it through its paces, try these tools out, compare them with each other, use them on your real data. Anyone can make a slick demo.
you're gonna wanna orchestrate it with some level of human decision making and control.
You want it to be repeatable and defensible

kp.k: Foundation models threaten thin intermediaries more than substantial platforms
kp.d: Responding to the host's question about foundation-model competition, Shankar argues that the recently publicised contract-review capability was not technically novel. He predicts greater adoption of general-purpose AI for simple transactional tasks and erosion of software primarily wrapping model capabilities. Conversely, he expects customers to continue paying for specialised infrastructure, operational reliability and accumulated workflow knowledge rather than rebuilding everything themselves. These are market forecasts supported by software analogies, not demonstrated market outcomes.
qs: That capability existed in LLMs well before that skill. Anyone could have done it.
I do think for those kinds of simple transactional tasks, you can use a Claude coworker, what have you, and it'll do a pretty good job. I suspect that that'll gain greater adoption.
if it's primarily a wrapper around these technologies, you will get eroded.
But if you've built real infrastructure at scale, I think people are going to want to pay for it because they're not going to want to build their own.

kp.k: Agents may interface with rather than replace specialised software
kp.d: Shankar uses spreadsheets as an analogy for general-purpose tools absorbing some tasks while specialised systems retain value through deeper functionality and checks and balances. He predicts AI agents will operate between users and robust software platforms, including automating browser actions, rather than eliminating enterprise software as a category.
qs: Excel is like the most versatile single application, maybe in the history of like, I don't know, software. And so it absorbed a lot of stuff that you might have used other software for.
You don't use Excel to do accounting, right? Because we need a lot more checks and balances, right?
I think you're gonna see these AI tools, even these AI agents, sit at the interface between the human. And then these very robust pieces of software that no one would want to replicate.

kp.k: Everlaw emphasises independent long-term platform development
kp.d: Shankar presents Everlaw as a litigation platform spanning legal holds, collections, discovery and post-discovery story building, with continuing non-AI development alongside AI investment. He says the company intends to keep building rather than pursue a specified exit, and attributes its capacity for long-term decisions to in-house development and the absence of majority owners or private equity. He reports about 550 employees in total, with approximately 350 in Oakland.
qs: It's upstream all the way up to legal holds, collections, and then core discovery, and then story building, right, which is post discovery.
every month we're shipping dozens of features
I think we just want to keep building the business.
all of our development work is done here in Oakland by our team.
the company has no majority owners, no PE, none of that stuff.
So about 550 total.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AJ Shankar claims generative AI materially expands litigation analysis and improves the speed and quality of review, while remaining one component of a broader human-and-technology toolkit.
pts.d: Shankar, Everlaw's founder and CEO, describes generative AI as a step change rather than simply an incremental improvement. He identifies existing uses including document summarisation, topic extraction, sentiment analysis, document questions, review-code suggestions, structured information extraction, deposition analysis, identification of conflicting testimony, memo drafting and statements of facts. Coding suggestions can apply a review rubric across thousands or tens of thousands of documents, explain proposed classifications and cite document passages for human checking. He frames these capabilities as augmentation of ongoing legal work, not autonomous replacement of litigators.

pts.k: Shankar claims Deep Dive makes targeted, corpus-wide factual investigation newly accessible and can uncover critical documents missed by earlier review.
pts.d: He describes a system that retrieves documents, extracts and ranks facts, and synthesises a cited answer to a question about the case corpus. His concrete example is obtaining an answer to a specific question within roughly a minute from a million-document collection, supporting deposition preparation or checking newly uploaded material for additional evidence. He distinguishes this targeted investigation from comprehensive responsiveness review. Compared with predictive coding, he says the tool requires neither specialised setup and training nor an already identified interesting document.

pts.k: Shankar claims document-grounded, narrowly designed AI applications reduce risk and improve performance relative to asking models for precise legal information from their training knowledge.
pts.d: He characterises generative AI as expressive and capable but less reliable than deterministic software. His preferred design uses bounded tasks, source citations and integration into existing workflows so users can verify answers. He says grounding improves performance, while asking a model to supply specific case law from its trained knowledge risks fabricated answers. Everlaw therefore confines its AI questions to supplied documents. This is a claim about relative reliability and product design, not a claim that grounded answers are error-free.

pts.k: Shankar predicts broader adoption of general-purpose AI for simple transactional tasks and competitive erosion of thin AI-wrapper software, but continued demand for substantial specialist infrastructure.
pts.d: Discussing foundation-model providers entering legal workflows, Shankar says an announced contract-review capability was already possible with existing models. He expects tools such as Claude to become routine for simple transactional work. He predicts agents embedded in operating systems and browsers will reduce the need for software that mainly intermediates simple actions. In contrast, he expects customers to keep paying for robust platforms offering scale, reliability, workflow knowledge and operational infrastructure. He envisages AI agents mediating between humans and such platforms rather than eliminating enterprise software. These are vendor-market predictions, not predictions of lawyer job losses.

pts.k: Shankar presents AI's effect on access to justice as conditional: unequal access could widen the gap, while access for under-resourced users could narrow it.
pts.d: He argues that powerful litigation tools can advantage parties with means if others cannot obtain them. Conversely, they can enable users without means to perform work they could not otherwise afford. He positions Everlaw's product-donation programme as part of addressing that risk, with the aim of making factual discovery more equally available in court.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is chiefly Shankar's product-development experience, reported customer use and anecdotes; the transcript supplies no formal accuracy or productivity benchmark.
pts.d: For coding suggestions, Shankar reports extensive use and strong performance without quantitative results. For Deep Dive, he reports deployment on hundreds of cases and customers finding previously missed critical documents; he offers to provide quotations and customer contacts, but no named matter or underlying documentation is supplied in the interview. The approximately one-minute response example is an illustrative capability claim, not a reported controlled test. Reliability claims are supported by his technical explanation of grounding and training knowledge, not measured hallucination rates or named sanctions cases. His market predictions rely on reasoning from Everlaw's infrastructure and customer experience, plus analogies to Microsoft Office, LibreOffice, spreadsheets and accounting software. For access to justice, he reports millions of dollars in donated product, but does not measure resulting legal outcomes or a reduction in unmet need.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Shankar distinguishes currently deployed capabilities from undated adoption predictions, expects human involvement to persist in the near term, and declines to predict life five or ten years ahead.
pts.d: In this interview labelled 2026, Shankar describes Deep Dive as released in December and already used on hundreds of cases. He anticipates additional capabilities during the interview year but gives no firm timetable for general-purpose agents' market effects. He explicitly limits Deep Dive to targeted questions rather than exhaustive responsiveness review and acknowledges imperfect answers. Effective deployment depends on task selection, supplied context, verification, user education, institutional risk tolerance and human decision-making. He recommends comparing products on actual customer data rather than relying on polished demonstrations. His access-to-justice prediction depends on who can obtain the technology.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are litigation practitioners and teams, legal-technology buyers and vendors, and under-resourced participants in the justice system.
pts.d: Litigators and document reviewers gain assistance with factual investigation, coding, deposition preparation and drafting, while retaining decisions about reliance and checking. Less technically specialised practitioners can ask corpus-wide questions without predictive-coding setup expertise. The broader platform serves law firms, in-house counsel and public-sector collaborators, although Shankar supplies no separate AI impact estimates for these groups. Buyers must assess tools against their own data and risk tolerance. Thin-wrapper vendors face predicted substitution by general-purpose AI and agents, whereas infrastructure-rich vendors are predicted to retain demand. Under-resourced users may gain affordable capacity or fall further behind better-equipped opponents depending on access. The interview makes no quantified claims about employment, staffing leverage, fees or lawyer displacement.
